title: What Sam Altman Really Thinks About the Future of Work
the_thought: He thinks AI will do the work, and people should get paid anyway.
hook: November, 2022. A chatbot goes live. By morning, people are pasting their own jobs into the box. Write the email. Finish the brief. Is this still work. Sam Altman built the box. Two years earlier he already wrote what happens next. He thinks AI will do the work, and people should get paid anyway. Then the Senate asked him about the future of work. He talked about better jobs on the other side.

levels.name: The Inbox
beats: The first week looks like a toy. Students cheat. Offices laugh. Then the laugh dies. A person who writes for a living watches the screen finish the paragraph. A person who codes watches it sketch the function. Nobody voted for this. It just shipped. Altman is not shocked. In March 2021, on a plain webpage, he wrote that software that can think and learn will do more and more of the work that people now do. He said even more power will shift from labor to capital. If public policy does not move, most people end up worse off than they are today. That is not a victory speech. That is a warning with a product attached. He is running the lab that is trying to make the warning come true. The inbox is the first proof. Thinking work, the kind that used to need a salary, now fits in a browser tab. People ask the obvious question. Will I still have a job. Managers ask a quieter one. How many chairs do we still need. He has two answers, and they do not live in the same room. One answer lives on a webpage. A check from taxed capital. The other answer lives in a hearing. Better jobs on the other side. The inbox does not tell you which one he means. It only shows you the work leaving. If the chairs go, the check is the only answer that still feeds you.

levels.name: The Essay
beats: Go back to that page. March 16, 2021. He calls it Moore's Law for Everything. He says in five years, programs that can think will read legal documents and give medical advice. In a decade they will do assembly-line work. After that they will do almost everything, even new science. Then the line that matters for work. The price of many kinds of labor will fall toward zero once powerful AI joins the workforce. Goods get cheap because labor was the cost. A house built by robots, from robots, costs what it costs to rent the machines. He says we will discover new jobs. We always do after a revolution. Because of the abundance on the other side, we will have freedom to be creative about what they are. People will still have jobs, he writes. Many of those jobs will not create a lot of economic value the way we think of value today. People get freed up to spend time with people they care about, to care for people, to look at art, to work toward social good. That is a soft landing. Then he builds the hard floor. Tax companies above a certain size 2.5 percent of their market value, paid in shares. Tax privately held land 2.5 percent, paid in dollars. Put it in a fund. Every citizen over 18 gets a yearly pile of cash and stock. He does the napkin math. In a decade, about 13,500 dollars a year for each adult, and it buys more because everything else got cheaper. He is not saying keep the job and add a bonus. He is saying the job stops being the thing that feeds you. The check does. A floor for everyone. A ceiling for no one. That is the social contract he put on the page before the chatbot existed. He even names the old fear. Plans that ignore this shift will fail the way feudal rules would fail in a factory town. He names the pile. An American Equity Fund. Not a charity basket. A slice of the companies that own the thinking machines. He is not asking a factory to keep extra hands for kindness. He is asking the country to tax the upside, then mail it. The wealth the software creates, he writes, can pay for the floor. Ownership, not a wage. That is the move hidden under the cheerful jobs talk.

levels.name: The Hearing
beats: May 16, 2023. A Senate room. Wood. Microphones. Cameras. A senator says his biggest nightmare is a new industrial revolution that wipes out millions of jobs. He wants to know if anyone is steering. Altman does not say the nightmare is fake. He says there will be a significant impact on jobs, and the shape is hard to predict. He tells them to treat the model as a tool, not a creature. He says it is good at tasks. Then he says the sharp sentence. GPT-4 will, he thinks, entirely automate away some jobs, and it will create new ones that they believe will be much better. He wants partnership. He also says the hard part is mostly for government: how to mitigate. His written testimony lists the mix. More productivity. Some new jobs. Some jobs changed. Some jobs gone. He talks about modernizing unemployment insurance. Adjustment assistance. Training for people in the line of fire. Listen to the gap. In 2021 the floor was a check from taxed capital. In 2023 the public answer is better jobs, plus a government landing pad. Same man. Same lab. Two registers. One for a webpage. One for a hearing that will be clipped by morning. He is not lying in either room. He is choosing which half of the essay to read out loud. The half that says we will find new work. Not the half that says labor's price falls toward zero and a fund replaces the wage. The room wants comfort. He gives them a tool, a better job, and a to-do list for Congress. He does not hold up the check. He does not read the tax plan into the record. He does not say labor falls toward zero. He says partnership. He says mitigate. The nightmare stays on the table. The check stays in the essay, where the cameras were not pointed.

levels.name: The Tasks
beats: Later the unit changes. Stop counting jobs, he says. Count tasks. A job is a bundle. The machine eats the bundle from the inside. He can easily imagine a world where a large share of the tasks in the economy get done by AI, not far from now. Forty percent is the number that gets repeated around him. The point is the direction. He talks about agents. A system that can work a day without a person hovering. Then a week. He says that out loud like it still surprises him. From our chair, he says, the result may look less like work than what we do now. He likes an old statistic. About every seventy-five years, half the jobs in a society turn over, even without this. He expects the turnover to run faster. Some jobs vanish. New ones appear that are hard to imagine from here, the way today's jobs would have looked strange from a farm. He has short-term worry. The crossing. Entry-level white-collar work. The first rungs. He has also said, when the rungs did not snap as fast as he feared, that he was glad to be wrong. That is not a retraction of the essay. It is a weather report. The storm can arrive late and still be the storm. What does not change is the bet. Machines take the tasks that used to justify a salary. People keep the parts that look like caring, wanting, learning how to learn. And if the salary thins out, the 2021 page already named the patch. The page is still there. The hearing clip is still there. The empty chair in the office is newer than both. A job title can survive while the work inside it dies. That is why he changed the unit. Agents do not apply for a role. They take the hours. The first rungs used to teach a person the job. If those rungs go, the ladder is still there. It just starts higher.

levels.name: The Check
beats: He helped start another project while the lab grew. A silver orb. A scan of an eye. A way to prove a person is a person in a world where machines can fake a face and a voice. The public fight around that project is messy. The idea underneath is simple. If cash is going to move without a boss, you still have to know who is real. He never passed the American Equity Fund. Congress did not vote him a dividend. The chatbot shipped anyway. The agents are shipping anyway. The inbox emptied anyway. So what does he really think about the future of work. He thinks AI will do the work, and people should get paid anyway. He will build the tools that eat the tasks. He will tell a hearing the jobs on the other side will be better. He will not treat the job as the thing that makes a life legitimate. The check was the point. The job was the old floor. He is trying to pour a new one. That is the future of work he keeps describing, even when he uses a softer word for the cameras. The orb is not a paycheck. It is a lock on a door he hopes someone else will put money behind. Until then, the inbox is the only part of the plan that shipped. The fund is still a page. The hearing is still a clip. The empty chair is the part you can touch.
What he thinks about who should own the machines is another story. That story is next.
